title: The Kitchen of the Crescent Cove
premise: Marine biologist Edmund Hartwell returns to Crescent Cove to settle his late aunt's estate, planning to sell the crumbling seaside kitchen-café and leave before his carefully contained heart can crack. But a letter postmarked eleven years ago—written by his aunt to the woman Edmund once loved and never stopped—surfaces behind the café's old oven, forcing him to confront the night he chose duty over love. As he restores the kitchen with the help of the café's ragtag regulars, he falls for Wren, the estate lawyer who keeps missing the last train, and learns that staying is not surrender. At the Cove's lantern festival, Edmund chooses found family over flight, keeping both the kitchen and the woman who stayed.
about_author: Beatrix Underhill is the pen name of a former pastry chef who traded midnight ovens for midnight manuscripts after twenty years of feeding small coastal towns. She writes love stories set in kitchens, convinced that every recipe is really a letter someone was too afraid to send.

chapters.title: Salt on the Deed
chapters.summary: Edmund arrives at Crescent Cove to inventory his aunt Marisol's estate, determined to list the café and be gone in two weeks. His guarded POV establishes his grief-disguised-as-efficiency. When he finds the kitchen still stocked with flour dated the week she died, the first hairline fracture opens: this was a home, not an asset.

chapters.title: The Lawyer Who Misses Trains
chapters.summary: Wren Okafor, the estate's local attorney, misses her train and ends up sharing Marisol's leftover lemon cake with Edmund in the dark kitchen. Her warm, wry POV contrasts his armor. The emotional beat is reluctant comfort—two strangers discovering the café makes honesty easier than either expected.

chapters.title: Inventory of Ghosts
chapters.summary: Cataloguing the café, Edmund finds a guestbook full of names he doesn't know but who clearly knew Marisol intimately. Through his POV we learn fragments of his own past: the woman named Ilse, the letter he never answered, the grant he took instead. Beat: guilt surfacing like something rising from deep water.

chapters.title: Behind the Old Oven
chapters.summary: Pulling out the ancient range to repair it, Edmund discovers a sealed envelope postmarked eleven years ago—Marisol's handwriting addressed to Ilse. His panic-driven POV shows him almost burning it unread. Instead he pockets it, unopened, as Wren watches him lie about what he found. Beat: the past gains weight.

chapters.title: Regulars
chapters.summary: Wren's POV: the café's found family—fisherman Dev, teenage runaway Poppy, insomniac baker Ruth—converge on Edmund, assuming he'll keep the place open through festival season. They teach him Marisol's recipes as inheritance. Edmund resists, then catches himself laughing. Beat: belonging arriving uninvited.

chapters.title: What the Letter Said
chapters.summary: Unable to sleep, Edmund finally reads Marisol's letter: she begged Ilse to come back, confessed that Edmund's silence broke them both, and asked forgiveness for urging him toward duty. His raw first-person reckoning reveals he chose the grant over Ilse because Marisol told him to secure his future. Beat: betrayal inverted—he was protecting her, and lost everything.

chapters.title: Rising Dough, Rising Stakes
chapters.summary: Edmund decides to reopen the café for the lantern festival, secretly hoping Ilse might come. Wren, falling for him, senses she's standing in someone else's story and pulls back; her hurt POV sharpens the triangle. A developer's offer on the property forces a deadline. Beat: love against duty, again, in a new key.

chapters.title: The Last Train Before the Festival
chapters.summary: Wren books a transfer to another town, taking the last train before festival weekend. Edmund, mid-confession, reaches the platform too late—or so he thinks. His desperate POV drives through rain to the next station. Beat: climax of pursuit; he finally says aloud that the heart is trainable, and hers is the only curriculum he wants.

chapters.title: Lanterns
chapters.summary: Festival night: the café glows, the regulars cook, and Ilse arrives—answering Marisol's eleven-year-old letter without knowing Edmund read it. Their closure scene, told in alternating POV, releases the old wound gently; Ilse is married, at peace, grateful. Edmund lights a lantern for Marisol. Beat: grief transmuted into gratitude.

chapters.title: After the Last Train Leaves
chapters.summary: Resolution in Wren's POV: she returns expecting goodbye and finds the deed re-titled to a community trust—with her name on the founding papers. Edmund asks her to stay not because the trains are unreliable, but because he finally is reliable. The kitchen fills with regulars, flour dust, and morning light. Beat: home chosen, openly, forever.
